units.title: Emergency Assessment and the First Minutes

lessons.title: Triage as a system: assigning priority when minutes matter
lessons.explanation: Triage is the method of assigning priority to emergency patients and their problems based on a rapid assessment of historical and physical parameters. It is not a guess about diagnosis, and it is not a queue. The working question is different: which patient, or which problem within a patient, will deteriorate soonest if attention does not reach it now. The veterinary literature makes this concrete by publishing lists rather than relying on intuition. Several historical or observed problems warrant transferring an animal to the treatment area regardless of what the physical examination shows, and all members of the veterinary team should be able to recognise them so that immediate veterinary evaluation can occur: allergic reaction with shock or airway obstruction, bleeding, cardiopulmonary arrest, collapse or inability to walk or loss of consciousness, difficulty or inability to urinate in male cats, dystocia, heatstroke, hypothermia, paleness or weakness, profuse vomiting, profuse diarrhoea, prolapsed or eviscerated organs, respiratory difficulty, seizures, substantial pain, snakebite, a swollen or painful abdomen with non-productive retching, toxin ingestion, and trauma or open wounds. Around that list sits a fixed structure for the first examination, the primary survey, whose components are conventionally remembered by the letters of the word eXsanguination, Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, and Exposure or environment. The sequence is a priority order, not an anatomical tour: bleeding and airway come before a detailed orthopaedic examination because those first two kill in minutes. Triage is also a system rather than a personal virtue. It works when there is a defined trigger, a named person who receives the report, and a time written down. A technician contributes detection, structured reporting and escalation; the assignment of a treatment plan is the veterinarian decision, and every threshold a team uses is a local clinical target rather than a rule a textbook can fix for an individual animal.
lessons.example: Three fictional patients arrive within four minutes of one another at 19:02, 19:04 and 19:06. The first is a young dog with a four centimetre skin laceration on the forelimb, bright and alert, taking treats from the owner. The second is a male cat that has been visiting the litter tray repeatedly and vocalising, with a tense abdomen. The third is a bulldog with loud, rasping breathing, an anxious expression, and a tongue that looks muddy purple rather than pink. Using the triage list rather than arrival order, the reasoning runs as follows. Respiratory difficulty and cyanosis place the bulldog first because airflow is the fastest route to death and noisy breathing with altered mucous membrane colour is an airway and breathing problem rather than a cosmetic one. Straining to urinate in a male cat appears on the list explicitly because an obstruction that is not relieved causes metabolic consequences that become difficult to reverse, so the cat is second. The laceration is a wound; it is unpleasant and it will need care, but the dog is stable, alert and eating, so it is third. Notice what the reasoning did not require: it did not require the technician to diagnose brachycephalic airway syndrome, urethral obstruction, or anything else. It required recognition of categories, a report in the order the observations were made, and an escalation with a time attached. A one sentence report such as, 19:06, bulldog, loud inspiratory noise, muddy tongue, sitting with elbows out, in treatment room now, gives the veterinarian everything needed to walk in and act.
lessons.question: Two patients are in the waiting room. A dog with an obviously deformed hindlimb is crying continuously and the owner is upset. A quiet cat sits in a carrier with pale gums, a capillary refill time of three seconds and no interest in the room. Which patient should be moved to the treatment area first, and why?
lessons.answer: The quiet cat, because pallor and a prolonged capillary refill time are perfusion findings that indicate shock, and shock outranks a limb fracture in the order of assessment even though the dog is making far more noise
lessons.distractor: The crying dog, because distress and visible deformity indicate the most urgent problem and the loudest patient is usually the sickest
lessons.correction: Triage sorts by physiological urgency, not by how much a patient expresses. Painful conditions are on the list of problems that warrant immediate veterinary evaluation, but a pale patient with delayed capillary refill is describing compromised oxygen delivery, which is a threat to life in minutes. Equating loudness with severity is the classic triage error, and it is the quiet, compensating patient who is most often missed.

depth.definitions: Triage is the assignment of priority to patients and problems by urgency rather than arrival time. The primary survey is the rapid stability examination structured as bleeding or eXsanguination, airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure or environment. The secondary survey is the thorough examination performed after stabilisation. Perfusion is the delivery of blood to tissue. Capillary refill time is the interval taken for colour to return to a blanched mucous membrane. Escalation is a defined act: a named recipient, a specific finding and a recorded time. Stat evaluation means the veterinarian is to attend immediately. Scope of practice is the legal and professional boundary of what a team member may decide alone; for a technician, recognition and reporting sit inside that boundary while treatment planning does not.
depth.mechanism: The triage method works because in a subset of conditions the interval between recognition and intervention dominates the outcome, and that subset is identifiable from a short list of cues rather than from a diagnosis. Airway and breathing problems kill through hypoxia, bleeding problems through loss of circulating volume, and obstruction or torsion problems through physiological cascades that become progressively harder to reverse. A fixed survey order turns that physiology into a repeatable behaviour that survives a busy room, an anxious owner and a tired team. Published lists also reduce a well documented failure mode of expert intuition: under time pressure people default to the most familiar or most recent pattern rather than to the most dangerous one. The limits matter as much as the method. Triage categories are provisional and are reassessed as information arrives, an animal can appear stable during a compensatory phase and decompensate quickly afterwards, and triage judgement is not a diagnosis. Uncertainty therefore belongs in the report, expressed as the observations that generated concern rather than as a clinical conclusion the reporter is not qualified to draw.
depth.secondExample: Consider a fictional dog with a swollen abdomen that arrives after a large meal and is retching without producing anything. It looks uncomfortable rather than dramatic, and it wags its tail when spoken to. A less structured approach might register tail wagging as reassurance and place this patient behind a dog with an actively bleeding ear. The structured approach does the opposite, because non-productive retching with a painful or distended abdomen appears on the published list of problems warranting transfer to the treatment area regardless of physical findings. The contrast teaches the general principle: behaviour such as tail wagging or eating is a genuine data point, but it is a data point about neurological and behavioural status, not a general certificate of stability. A second contrast concerns a fictional cat with a hindlimb limp after a fall from a window. It looks stable and the visible problem is a limb, yet the hidden risk in high rise falls is an internal injury pattern that accompanies the apparent orthopaedic problem. That is why a full triage survey is performed on every trauma patient rather than only on the dramatic ones.
depth.mistake: A frequent misconception is that triage means deciding what is wrong with the patient, so a technician who cannot name the condition feels unable to triage. The diagnostic correction is that triage assigns priority to problems, not names to diseases; the published lists are lists of complaints and findings that any staff member can recognise, so that immediate veterinary evaluation follows. A second misconception is that triage is complete once, at the door. Triage is a repeating activity, because patients move between categories in both directions, and an animal that was stable on arrival can become unstable during a long wait. A third is the belief that a long wait proves a low priority. A queue is evidence about resources, not about physiology, and a practice that never re-checks waiting patients converts a resource problem into a clinical one.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Write a three line escalation report for each of the following fictional scenarios, using the format: time, signalment, observed findings with numbers where you have them, requested action. Scenario one: a cat presented for a limp, whose respiratory rate you count as 40 breaths in 30 seconds and whose gums are pale. Scenario two: a dog presented for vomiting once, alert and drinking, with a heart rate of 160 and pink gums. Then compare your reports with this model response for scenario one. At 16:20, domestic shorthair cat, reported limp, respiratory rate 40 in 30 seconds which is 80 breaths per minute, pale mucous membranes, no interest in the room, please assess now. Self review rubric, four points. Did you include a time. Did you translate a count into a rate per minute and state your counting interval. Did you state the observation rather than a diagnosis. Did you name the specific action you needed from the veterinarian rather than describing your worry. Score your own report against those four criteria before comparing with the model.
depth.summary: Triage is a system of priority assignment built from published lists and a fixed survey order, designed to be used by every member of a clinical team rather than only by the clinician. The transferable skill is the habit of asking which problem deteriorates soonest, of translating observations into a short report with numbers and times, and of escalating to a named person. The limits are equally transferable: priority can change, appearance can mislead in both directions, and the report is a request for veterinary judgement rather than a substitute for it.

visual.title: Priority by physiology, not by arrival or noise
visual.description: A four column diagram that routes three arriving patients through the same decision sequence and lands them in an order determined by threat to bleeding, airway, breathing and circulation rather than by how dramatic they look.
steps: Column one, arrival log: patient A, alert dog with a limb laceration; patient B, male cat straining to urinate; patient C, bulldog with loud breathing and a muddy tongue.
Column two, the first question asked of each patient: is there bleeding, airway compromise or breathing failure that would kill within minutes.

Column three, category assignment using the published list: respiratory difficulty and altered mucous membrane colour for patient C, difficulty urinating in a male cat for patient B, trauma or open wounds for patient A.
Column four, action and record: report each finding to the veterinarian with a clock time, keep patient A under observation while B and C are seen, and re-triage all three if the wait lengthens.

lessons.title: Airway and breathing: the first two letters that change everything
lessons.explanation: Once bleeding has been addressed, two questions govern the next minutes: whether air can reach the lungs, and whether it is reaching them usefully. The veterinary literature separates these deliberately. Airway problems are problems of the conducting passages, meaning the nose, pharynx, larynx, cervical trachea, intrathoracic trachea and bronchi. Breathing problems are problems of the pleural space, the chest wall, the alveoli and the control of ventilation. The distinction is not academic, because the findings differ and so does the response. Compromise of the extrathoracic airway, meaning the nasal passages, pharynx, larynx or cervical trachea, produces inspiratory difficulty and inspiratory stridor, a harsh noise on drawing breath in. Compromise of the intrathoracic trachea or the bronchi produces expiratory stridor. Stertor is a snoring, low pitched sound most often associated with the pharynx and nasal cavities. Complete large airway obstruction is a different state again: such animals are unconscious and apneic and require immediate cardiopulmonary resuscitation and tracheal intubation. For the partially obstructed patient the published practical guidance is unglamorous and important. The first priority is oxygen therapy delivered with minimal stress, and the fastest option in most cases is flow-by oxygen, which also allows examination to continue. A small animal placed in an oxygen cage or chamber receives a low stress supply of oxygen, but the cage limits access and can delay reassessment. Categorising the distress as upper airway or lower airway shapes what happens next: loud inspiratory noise, anxiety and sometimes cyanosis suggest an upper airway problem, while a different pattern of loud sounds on auscultation suggests pulmonary or pleural disease. One rule is repeated because it protects patients: severely dyspnoeic animals should not be taken for radiography before stabilisation, and where air or fluid in the pleural space is suspected, thoracocentesis to relieve the signs and to identify air versus fluid takes precedence over radiography. The technician work here is oxygen set-up, minimal and considered handling, continuous observation, and accurate reporting of pattern, rate and effort. Any decision to sedate, to place a needle in the chest or to intubate belongs to the veterinarian.
lessons.example: A fictional seven year old pug is carried in at 08:12 with a history of louder than usual breathing since the previous evening and one episode of collapse. The technician observes the patient without touching it first. The breathing is audible from the doorway, the noise is heard on inspiration, and the tongue is grey purple at the edges. The respiratory rate counted over 15 seconds is 14 breaths, which is 56 breaths per minute. The dog stands with its elbows out and its neck extended, and it resists being laid down. Reasoning from the pattern rather than from a diagnosis: a noise audible without a stethoscope, loudest on inspiration, with a dog holding an extended neck, sits in the upper airway category. The first action is the least invasive useful one, which is flow-by oxygen delivered with the tubing held near the open mouth while the veterinarian is called, because stress increases oxygen demand at exactly the moment supply is limited. The next action is to avoid making matters worse: do not place the patient on its back for radiographs, do not apply a muzzle to a dyspnoeic animal, do not struggle with a jugular blood draw in a patient that cannot spare the oxygen, and do not leave to prepare a cage while nobody watches the breathing. The report to the veterinarian runs: 08:14, pug, inspiratory noise audible without stethoscope, tongue grey purple, respiratory rate 56 per minute counted over 15 seconds, standing with elbows out, flow-by oxygen started, please come now. The technician does not need to know whether the lesion is laryngeal, tracheal or something else; the pattern, the rate and the colour are enough to change what happens next.
lessons.question: You are asked to triage a fictional dyspnoeic patient and the veterinary practice has a radiography room ten metres from the waiting area. The patient has an audible inspiratory noise, marked abdominal effort and a respiratory rate of 60 breaths per minute. Which plan best reflects the published emergency guidance?
lessons.answer: Provide oxygen with minimal stress, keep handling to the minimum, and have the veterinarian assess immediately, with thoracocentesis prioritised over radiography if pleural space disease is suspected
lessons.distractor: Take the patient for thoracic radiographs at once, because imaging is the fastest way to establish a diagnosis and the room is close
lessons.correction: The emergency guidance is explicit that stress and restraint worsen these patients and that severely dyspnoeic animals should not be radiographed before stabilisation. In suspected pleural space disease, thoracocentesis relieves the signs and distinguishes air from fluid, and it takes precedence over imaging. Moving an unstable patient through a practice to obtain pictures inverts the order of risk: the diagnostic image is not worth the arrest.

depth.definitions: Dyspnoea is laboured or difficult breathing. Orthopnoea is breathlessness that is worse when lying down, which is why some patients adopt particular postures. Stridor is a harsh inspiratory or expiratory sound indicating turbulent flow in a narrowed large airway. Stertor is a lower pitched snoring sound typical of pharyngeal or nasal disease. Cyanosis is a blue or grey purple colour of mucous membranes reflecting a severe reduction in oxygenated haemoglobin. Flow-by oxygen is oxygen delivered from tubing held near the nose or mouth. Thoracocentesis is the placement of a needle or catheter into the pleural space to remove air or fluid, a veterinarian procedure. Pulse oximetry estimates haemoglobin oxygen saturation and must never delay care. Auscultation is listening with a stethoscope.
depth.mechanism: The upper and lower airway distinction follows from where resistance lies and when the pressure gradient is greatest. When the extrathoracic airway narrows, pressure inside the airway falls during inspiration while pressure outside does not, so the segment collapses further and the sound is inspiratory. When the intrathoracic airway narrows, compression occurs mainly during expiration, so the noise is expiratory. Turbulent flow through a narrowed segment generates sound, so noise audible without a stethoscope implies substantial turbulence somewhere proximal. Oxygen delivery fails differently in each category. An obstructed airway limits entry of gas, while pleural air or fluid prevents lung expansion mechanically, and pulmonary disease disrupts gas exchange across the membrane. That is why a normal oxygen supply can coexist with severe hypoxaemia, and why assessment is a pattern problem rather than a single measurement. Handling adds a second insult through fear, restraint and pain, each of which raises oxygen consumption and can tip a compensating patient into failure. The mechanism also explains why relieving a pleural space improves a patient within moments, and why sedatives are useful in some airway patients but risky in others: they reduce oxygen demand and struggle, but can also blunt the drive that is keeping the patient ventilating. That balance is a veterinary judgement.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the pug with a fictional domestic shorthair cat presented with a two week history of coughing that the owner attributes to hairballs, and a respiratory rate of 44 breaths per minute while sitting quietly. This cat shows exaggerated abdominal effort, and auscultation reveals loud sounds throughout the thorax. Here the published categorisation points towards a small airway or pulmonary problem rather than an obstructive large airway lesion, and the auscultation findings are described as loud rather than quiet. That changes the immediate question from keeping an obstructed airway open to whether gas exchange is compromised and whether the cat needs oxygen, sedation or further assessment. In a third variation, a fictional dog with a chest wound and a respiratory rate of 50 per minute has quiet auscultation and an exaggerated abdominal effort alternating with exaggerated chest excursions, a pattern that raises the possibility of pneumothorax or pleural effusion; in that patient the reported guidance is to consider thoracocentesis before radiography. Three patients, three patterns, one habit of careful description.
depth.mistake: The common misconception is that loud breathing means serious disease and quiet breathing means safety, so a noisy brachycephalic dog is dismissed as normal for the breed while a quietly deteriorating patient is ignored. The diagnostic correction is to assess pattern, effort, rate, colour and posture together, and to recognise that altered colour and posture with a high rate are more ominous than the volume of the sound. A second misconception is that oxygen is a treatment and therefore the endpoint. Oxygen buys time while the cause is addressed, and it can delay the only action that helps in some cases if it becomes a reason to postpone thoracocentesis or airway assessment. A third is the belief that an anxious dyspnoeic animal needs calming with restraint. Restraint is the opposite of what such a patient needs; calm handling, minimal intervention and a prepared team reduce stress, and chemical sedation requires veterinary selection.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. With veterinary supervision, observe three patients or three clinical videos and describe each using only this framework: whether a noise is present and in which phase of breathing it occurs, respiratory rate counted over fifteen seconds and converted to a rate per minute, posture, mucous membrane colour, and estimated effort. Then write one sentence per patient stating which category you would report and what you would ask for. Self review rubric, five points. Did you record a counting interval for every rate. Did you convert the count accurately, for example 11 breaths in 15 seconds becoming 44 per minute. Did you state the phase of breathing rather than only the presence of noise. Did you record colour and posture. Did you avoid naming a disease. Mark each point out of one for a total of five.
depth.summary: Airway and breathing are the second and third items of the primary survey because airflow failure kills quickly, and the useful clinical skill is pattern description rather than naming a disease. Inspiratory noise points towards the extrathoracic airway, expiratory noise towards the intrathoracic airway, and quiet chests with a struggling pattern towards pleural space disease. The transferable habit is to supply oxygen with minimal stress, to avoid restraint, and to avoid moving an unstable patient for diagnostics, while recognising that the relief procedures themselves are veterinary decisions.

visual.title: Pattern before name: describing a dyspnoeic patient
visual.description: A flow diagram that begins with a patient in respiratory difficulty and branches according to audible pattern, phase of breathing and auscultation, ending in a reported category and a requested action rather than a diagnosis.
steps: Start: patient with increased respiratory effort. Count the rate over 15 seconds, note the posture, note the mucous membrane colour.

Branch one, noise audible without a stethoscope on inspiration: describe as inspiratory stridor with an extrathoracic airway pattern, start flow-by oxygen with minimal handling, request immediate veterinary assessment.
Branch two, noise on expiration: describe as expiratory stridor or expiratory effort, suspect intrathoracic or lower airway involvement, keep the patient calm and oxygenated.

Branch three, no noise but marked effort with quiet auscultation and alternating abdominal and chest excursions: report suspected pleural space disease and expect thoracocentesis to precede radiography.
End: report pattern, rate, colour, posture and the action requested, and do not name a diagnosis you are not qualified to make.

lessons.title: Shock recognition and perfusion assessment
lessons.explanation: Shock is a state in which perfusion is inadequate to meet the oxygen and metabolic demands of tissue. It is a description of delivery failure rather than a diagnosis, and it has several causes that call for different responses. In hypovolaemic or haemorrhagic shock, circulating volume is lost. In distributive shock, the problem is abnormal distribution of flow and loss of vascular tone, so tissue may be underperfused even while extremities feel warm. In cardiogenic shock, the pump itself is failing. In obstructive shock, flow is impeded mechanically as with a tension pneumothorax or a pericardial constraint. The veterinary manual makes the physiology explicit: when loss of volume lowers vessel wall tension, baroreceptor firing falls, the medulla reduces its inhibition of the sympathetic system, and the results are seen clinically as changes in heart rate, pulse intensity, blood pressure, capillary refill time, mucous membrane colour, level of consciousness and rectal temperature. Those physical perfusion parameters, combined with blood pressure, are how an intravascular volume deficit is detected. Measured parameters add objective data for reaching resuscitation endpoints and for monitoring trends, and direct or indirect arterial blood pressure, central venous pressure, central venous oxygen measurements and serum lactate concentration are named for that purpose. Shock progresses through stages. In the early compensatory stage of hypovolaemic shock, animals are often tachycardic with pink to red mucous membranes and a rapid capillary refill time; as compensation is exhausted, decompensation brings bradycardia in some patients, prolonged refill times, pale or muddy membranes and altered mentation. The technician role is to measure the same parameters the same way each time, to record the time of each set, to recognise a trend rather than a single reading, and to escalate to the veterinarian. Every substitution decision, and every volume decision, belongs to the veterinarian.
lessons.example: A fictional eight year old spaniel is presented at 21:40 after being hit by a car. Observations are taken at 21:40, 22:10 and 22:40 using the same technique, with the counting interval and the cuff position recorded each time. At 21:40 the heart rate is 150 beats per minute, capillary refill time is one second, membranes are pink, and the dog is bright but anxious. At 22:10 the heart rate is 170, capillary refill time is two seconds, membranes are pink but tacky, and the dog is quieter. At 22:40 the heart rate is 190, capillary refill time is three seconds, membranes are pale, and the dog does not lift its head when spoken to. Three arithmetic observations make the trend reportable rather than vague. The heart rate rose from 150 to 190 beats per minute, which is an increase of 40 beats per minute, or 26.7 percent above the first value. The capillary refill time lengthened from one second to three seconds, a threefold change. The reported lactate rose from 2.1 to 4.8 millimoles per litre, an increase of 2.7, or about 128.6 percent above the first value. Nothing in that set names a diagnosis and none of it is a technician decision. What it does is describe a trajectory: the same parameters measured the same way are moving in the direction of decompensation. The report to the veterinarian is one sentence with the numbers and the times, and the patient stays under continuous observation rather than being left with the paperwork.
lessons.question: A fictional dog recovering from a road traffic accident has warm extremities, deep red mucous membranes, a rapid capillary refill time and a bounding pulse, but the measured blood pressure is low. Which interpretation is most consistent with the physiology taught here?
lessons.answer: The findings suggest a distributive or early compensatory picture with vasodilatation and increased pulse pressure, and the combination of warm periphery with a low measured pressure is exactly why physical findings alone are not treated as reassurance
lessons.distractor: Warm extremities and a bounding pulse show that perfusion is adequate, so the low blood pressure reading can be attributed to an inaccurate cuff and discounted
lessons.correction: Warm extremities indicate that blood is reaching the periphery, not that it is reaching it in adequate quantity, and a bounding pulse reflects an increased pulse pressure during a hyperdynamic compensatory state. The manual lists bounding or hyperdynamic pulses as a feature of the compensatory stage of shock and weak or absent pulses as a feature of reduced cardiac output. Discounting a measured value because the physical examination looks reassuring removes the very data that detects the problem.

depth.definitions: Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion relative to demand. Hypovolaemic shock follows loss of circulating volume, haemorrhagic shock is the bleeding form of it, distributive shock involves abnormal distribution of flow or loss of vascular tone, cardiogenic shock originates in pump failure, and obstructive shock follows mechanical impediment to flow. Perfusion is delivery of blood to tissue. Compensatory stage is the phase in which homeostatic mechanisms maintain perfusion to vital organs at the expense of others; decompensatory stage is the phase in which those mechanisms fail. Pulse pressure is the difference between systolic and diastolic pressure. A pulse deficit is a difference between the heartbeats counted and the pulses palpated. Lactate is a marker whose interpretation depends on perfusion, metabolic state and sample handling, and which the manual uses for trends and resuscitation endpoints rather than as a single decisive number.
depth.mechanism: The signs of shock are the observable output of a specific reflex chain. Reduced vessel wall tension lowers stimulation of baroreceptors in the aortic arch and carotid bodies, which reduces afferent firing through the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves to the medulla, which in turn releases the sympathetic system from inhibition. Sympathetic activity raises heart rate and contractility, constricts peripheral vessels to preserve central pressure, and redirects flow towards brain and heart. This is why the same underlying problem can present as tachycardia with pink membranes and a fast refill early, and as a decompensating patient with prolonged refill, pallor and altered mentation later. It also explains why a measured blood pressure can remain near normal until compensation fails, and why a normal reading is not a certificate of adequate perfusion. Trends are more informative than thresholds because individual animals vary and because the direction of travel shows whether compensation is holding. The limits are inherent: physical parameters are subjective between observers, cuff size and technique alter blood pressure readings, and lactate reflects many processes in addition to hypoperfusion. That is precisely why a technician records method alongside value.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the trauma patient with a fictional dog presented after a bee sting with hives, vomiting, and collapse. This dog has red mucous membranes, a very fast capillary refill, warm limbs and a weak, rapid pulse, and the measured blood pressure is low. The mechanism here is distributive: vascular tone has fallen and flow is being misdirected, so the periphery is warm while effective perfusion pressure is inadequate, and an allergic reaction with evidence of shock appears on the triage list of problems warranting immediate veterinary evaluation. The physical findings look superficially better than the pale, cold patient, yet the physiology is at least as dangerous. A third variation is the fictional cat with a muffled heart sound, distended jugular pulse and poor perfusion, in which the mechanism is obstructive or cardiogenic and where a large volume of fluid would be the wrong response rather than the right one. Three patients with the same word, shock, and three different mechanisms, which is why the category matters and why the response is a veterinary decision.
depth.mistake: The most common misconception is that shock is defined by low blood pressure and can be excluded by a normal reading. The manual explains that physical perfusion parameters are combined with blood pressure precisely because each alone is insufficient, and that a compensatory patient may hold pressure while sacrificing peripheral perfusion. A second misconception is that shock is always cold and pale. Distributive shock can present with warm extremities and injected membranes, and cats in particular may show bradycardia rather than tachycardia, so a template picture is unreliable. A third misconception is that a single improved reading means recovery. Resuscitation endpoints exist because one number can improve while the patient remains underperfused, so the endpoint set rather than a single value is what the team evaluates, and it is the team, led by the veterinarian, that defines it.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Using a fictional case sheet that provides three sets of observations at 21:40, 22:10 and 22:40, calculate the percentage change in heart rate and the absolute change in capillary refill time, then write the escalation sentence you would say out loud. Model response: heart rate increased from 150 to 190 beats per minute, which is 40 beats per minute or 26.7 percent, capillary refill time lengthened from one to three seconds, mucous membranes changed from pink to pale, mentation changed from bright to unresponsive to voice, all three sets taken with the same method, please assess now. Self review rubric, five points. One point for stating the interval between measurements. One point for reporting both the absolute and the percentage change. One point for stating that the method was consistent. One point for describing mentation and membrane colour as findings. One point for requesting a specific action from a named person rather than expressing concern in general terms.
depth.summary: Shock is inadequate perfusion relative to demand, and it is recognised through a defined set of physical and measured parameters rather than through a single number. The mechanism is a baroreceptor driven sympathetic response that compensates at first and then fails, which is why trends and combinations outperform isolated readings, and why a warm, pink, tachycardic patient can be as compromised as a cold and pale one. The transferable skill is disciplined serial measurement with the method recorded, an honest report of direction of travel, and escalation, while classification and treatment remain veterinary decisions.

visual.title: Same parameters, three time points: reading a perfusion trend
visual.description: A timeline diagram with three vertical assessment columns at 21:40, 22:10 and 22:40, each containing heart rate, capillary refill time, mucous membrane colour and mentation, with arrows showing the direction of change and a final box that contains the single escalation sentence.
steps: Column one, 21:40. Heart rate 150 beats per minute, capillary refill one second, membranes pink, mentation bright. Label the stage as compensating.

lessons.title: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation fundamentals and the technician role
lessons.explanation: Cardiopulmonary arrest is a state in which the heart and lungs have stopped providing circulation and ventilation, and cardiopulmonary resuscitation is the organised response. The veterinary literature explains why preparation dominates technique. The RECOVER initiative, supported by the American College of Veterinary Emergency and Critical Care and the Veterinary Emergency and Critical Care Society, produced the first consensus guidelines in 2012 and updated them in 2024; the guidelines divide resuscitation into five domains, which are prevention and preparedness, basic life support, advanced life support, monitoring, and post cardiac arrest care. Survival is low and worth stating honestly: the RECOVER initiative reports that fewer than six percent of dogs and fewer than twenty percent of cats that experience cardiopulmonary arrest survive to hospital discharge, and the veterinary manual reports small survival figures for dogs and cats alongside a much higher reported rate of return of spontaneous circulation. It also notes that animals whose arrest is associated with anaesthesia have a better prognosis. Recognition is the first skill. The recommended immediate check is the shake and shout to determine responsiveness, and palpation of pulses is explicitly not recommended before starting compressions because it delays intervention. With a single rescuer, compressions begin immediately and are combined with ventilations if there is no risk of zoonotic transmission, at a ratio of thirty compressions to two breaths; in hospital, intubation should occur early and compressions should not be stopped to place the tube if that can be avoided. The compressions themselves have published parameters: a rate of 100 to 120 per minute regardless of patient size, a depth of one third to one half of the width of the chest wall for patients in lateral recumbency and one quarter for dorsal recumbency, and full recoil between compressions. Compressions run for two minutes, which is called one cycle, without interruption, because it takes about a minute of continuous compressions before myocardial perfusion pressure reaches its maximum. It is important to state the limit plainly: even with ideal technique, only a maximum of about thirty percent of normal cardiac output can be achieved. After any resuscitation event, a debrief is recommended, lasting five to ten minutes with the team leader, asking what went well, what could have been done better, and what needs reporting. The technician role spans equipment readiness, high quality compressions, recording, ventilation support, catheter and drug preparation under direction, closed loop communication, and participation in training and debrief. Which drugs are given, and when resuscitation is stopped, are veterinary decisions.
lessons.example: A fictional ten year old dog arrests at 11:02 during a dental procedure, while already intubated and connected to a monitor. The team has a crash cart and has practised the sequence. Arithmetic helps show what two good minutes look like. At a rate of 110 compressions per minute, one two minute cycle contains 220 compressions; at the guideline range of 100 to 120 per minute, one cycle contains between 200 and 240. A rescuer who pauses for ten seconds per minute to check a pulse reduces the cycle to 200 compressions at best and interrupts the perfusion pressure that took a minute to build, which is why the guideline treats interruptions as the main enemy of compression quality. Roles are assigned out loud: one person compresses, one ventilates with oxygen through the secured tube, one records events and timings, one manages the intravenous catheter and prepares what the veterinarian asks for, and the veterinarian leads and decides. Each recorded item carries a time, for example arrest recognised 11:02, compressions started 11:02, ventilation started 11:03, first cycle completed 11:04, intravenous access confirmed 11:05. The compressor is changed at the cycle boundary rather than mid cycle, and the change takes seconds. Afterwards the team debriefs for ten minutes and reviews the record, including the interval between recognition and the first compression, which was zero in this case because the patient was already monitored and the team had rehearsed. The point of the example is that most of what made those minutes good happened before the arrest.
lessons.question: A fictional patient collapses in a practice without a crash cart and without practised roles. A single technician finds the animal unresponsive. Which action sequence best reflects the published basic life support guidance?
lessons.answer: Confirm unresponsiveness with a shake and shout, call for help immediately, and start chest compressions at once without delaying to palpate a pulse, adding ventilations at the recommended ratio if a single rescuer is present
lessons.distractor: Palpate the femoral pulse for a full minute to be certain the patient has arrested, then begin compressions once the absence of a pulse is documented
lessons.correction: The guidance states that palpation of pulses is not recommended before initiating compressions because it delays intervention and because pulse assessment is unreliable even for experienced staff. Recognition is clinical and immediate: unresponsive to a shake and shout means compressions start now while help is called. Documenting a pulse deficit is not the entry ticket to resuscitation.

depth.definitions: Cardiopulmonary arrest is cessation of effective circulation and ventilation. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation is the coordinated response to it. Basic life support covers compressions and ventilation, and advanced life support covers interventions such as vascular access, monitoring and drugs. Return of spontaneous circulation is the restoration of a detectable circulation. The five guideline domains are prevention and preparedness, basic life support, advanced life support, monitoring, and post cardiac arrest care. A cycle is two minutes of uninterrupted compressions. Closed loop communication is a request that is repeated back and confirmed. Debriefing is a short structured review after an event. A cognitive aid is a checklist or algorithm designed to be used during an event rather than memorised.
depth.mechanism: Two mechanisms are described for generating forward flow. In the cardiac pump technique, direct compression of the ventricles moves blood; in the thoracic pump technique, changes in intrathoracic pressure move it. Both depend on an intact closed chest and on full recoil, because recoil creates the pressure difference that refills the heart, which is why leaning on the chest between compressions is treated as a defect. The reason a two minute cycle exists is arithmetic plus physiology: myocardial perfusion pressure accumulates over about a minute of continuous compressions, so frequent interruptions repeatedly return the patient to the beginning of that curve. The reason the rate is specified irrespective of size is that optimal compression frequency is a property of the circulation rather than of the patient dimensions, while depth is scaled to chest width. The reason preparedness dominates is that arrest is rare, sudden and highly time sensitive, so performance depends on rehearsed roles, standardised equipment and cognitive aids rather than on recall under stress. The limits are real: compression quality is difficult to sustain, survival to discharge is low, and hands-on training has been shown to improve technique particularly in novices, which is an argument for practice rather than confidence.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the monitored dental arrest with a fictional arrest that happens in a car park at a vaccination appointment, with no crash cart, one trained technician and the veterinarian thirty seconds away. Here the same basic principles apply but the constraints change. The technician confirms unresponsiveness, calls for help, and starts compressions without waiting, using the same rate and depth parameters, and ventilation is provided with a tight fitting mask rather than through a tube. The outcome may be unchanged by anything the team does; the manual notes that prognosis depends on the underlying cause, the timeliness and effectiveness of intervention, and the preparedness of the team. The lesson is not that the car park event was handled badly, but that the practise of the crash cart, the algorithms on the wall and the rehearsal of roles is what converts an unlikely event into a survivable one. A third variation is the arrest in a patient with a known terminal disease and a documented decision not to attempt resuscitation, where the appropriate action is to follow the documented plan and support the client. That plan is made by the veterinarian with the owner, in advance, never by a technician in the moment.
depth.mistake: A common misconception is that resuscitation should wait for the veterinarian because compressions are a medical act. The guidance places compressions first and specifies that help should be called simultaneously rather than sequentially, and every minute without compressions is a minute of no circulation. A second misconception is that pausing compressions to intubate or to place a catheter is harmless because it is brief. The manual states that compressions should not be discontinued for intubation where that can be avoided, and the mechanism of perfusion pressure accumulation explains why. A third misconception is that a training certificate equals competence, or that a successful outcome proves good technique. Skill decays, technique is measurable, and the RECOVER courses themselves require periodic renewal. A fourth is the belief that a fast heartbeat after return of circulation means the patient is safe; post arrest care is its own domain precisely because return of circulation is a beginning rather than an ending.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Without touching a live patient, rehearse a two minute cycle with a manikin or a padded surface, a metronome and a stopwatch, and keep a written log. Record the target rate you set, the number of compressions you actually delivered in each thirty second block, and the length of any interruption. Then compute the total for the two minutes and compare with the arithmetic benchmark: at 110 per minute a clean cycle contains 220 compressions, and at the guideline range of 100 to 120 per minute it contains between 200 and 240. Model reflection: my first thirty second block contained 54 compressions, which is 108 per minute, and I paused for four seconds to reposition, giving 216 in the cycle. Self review rubric, four points. Did you state your counting interval and how you counted. Did you identify at least one specific interruption and its length. Did you compute totals with a tool or on paper rather than estimating. Did you identify one change you would make next time, stated as a behaviour rather than as an intention to try harder.
depth.summary: Resuscitation is organised around a small number of physiological facts: circulation needs compressions at a defined rate and depth, perfusion pressure needs uninterrupted cycles, and effective ventilation needs a secure airway with confirmed placement. Around those facts sits a system of preparedness, assigned roles, recorded times, cognitive aids and structured debriefing, and that system is where technicians make the largest contribution. The honest limits are that survival to discharge remains low, that technique is a trainable skill rather than a stable trait, and that decisions about interventions and about stopping belong to the veterinarian.

lessons.title: Wound classification and the boundaries of first aid
lessons.explanation: The first step in wound management is not the wound. The veterinary manual is blunt about it: assessment of the overall stability of the animal comes first, because an obvious open wound can distract attention from more subtle but potentially life threatening problems such as shock. Only after that assessment is the patient stabilised, and only then is first aid for the wound performed as soon as it is safely possible. The mechanics of first aid for haemorrhage are specific. Active bleeding is controlled with direct pressure. For severe arterial bleeding the manual recommends a pneumatic cuff or a pressure wrap rather than a tourniquet, inflated until haemorrhage is controlled, because a narrow tourniquet carries a risk of neurovascular complications. The wound is then protected from further contamination or trauma by covering it with a sterile, lint free dressing. Describing a wound uses a small vocabulary. A laceration is a cut, a puncture is a narrow penetrating injury, an abrasion is a superficial scrape, an avulsion or degloving injury separates skin from underlying tissue, and a bite wound is a crush injury with a small surface opening and a large area of damaged deeper tissue. Wounds are also described by contamination, from surgically clean through contaminated to dirty and infected, and by the time elapsed since injury, because bacterial load increases with time. Lavage, meaning washing, serves two purposes: it removes visible and microscopic debris, which lowers bacterial load, and it allows better examination of underlying tissue. The published guidance is that large volumes matter more than additives, that the pressure matters, and that the ideal fluid is antiseptic without being toxic to healing tissue; saline is the least toxic, surgical scrub agents should not be used because the detergents damage tissue, stronger chlorhexidine concentrations are toxic to healing tissue, and hydrogen peroxide is toxic to healthy tissue and should not be used for wound lavage. The technician boundaries are as important as the technique. First aid covers haemorrhage control, covering, immobilising where appropriate, keeping the patient warm, and documentation of what was done and when. It does not cover exploring a wound with a probe or a finger, removing an embedded object, closing a wound, choosing an antimicrobial or deciding on debridement. Analgesia, culture, antimicrobial selection and definitive wound care are veterinary or veterinary directed decisions, and every patient needs a veterinarian assessment however tidy the wound looks.
lessons.example: A fictional terrier is presented at 17:05 with a bite wound to the left flank sustained during a walk at 15:40, which is an elapsed interval of 85 minutes. On arrival the dog is bright, its gums are pink, capillary refill time is one second, heart rate is 130 and it is weight bearing normally. The technician records those stability findings first, because they are the reason the wound will be managed as a wound rather than as part of a resuscitation. The wound itself is a 2 centimetre skin puncture with a surrounding area of swelling and two small abrasions. Reasoning about classification: the surface opening is small, but a bite is a crush injury, so the visible size understates the injured tissue, and the wound is contaminated rather than clean. Reasoning about first aid: there is no active bleeding, so no pressure wrap is needed beyond the dressing already applied by the owner. The wound is covered with a sterile lint free dressing rather than being scrubbed. Lavage is not attempted with a surgical scrub or with hydrogen peroxide, both of which the manual identifies as damaging to healing tissue; if the veterinarian asks for lavage, the parameters are a large volume at a controlled pressure, with saline as the least toxic choice. What the technician does next is exactly what the manual supports: keep the patient warm, keep the dressing in place, document the time of injury, the mechanism, the dressing applied, the stability findings at 17:05 and the exact time the veterinarian was told. The most consequential thing a technician can do for a bite wound is to prevent it from being treated as a small hole.
lessons.question: A fictional dog arrives with active bleeding from a paw laceration after a shattered glass injury. The dog is stable, alert and pink. Which action belongs within technician first aid, as described in the emergency guidance?
lessons.answer: Apply firm direct pressure and, if bleeding continues, use a pressure wrap rather than a narrow tourniquet, cover the wound with a sterile lint free dressing, and report to the veterinarian with the time bleeding started and the measures used
lessons.distractor: Irrigate the wound with hydrogen peroxide, scrub the edges with surgical scrub to reduce contamination, then apply a tight bandage to stop the bleeding before seeking veterinary assessment
lessons.correction: Hydrogen peroxide is identified as toxic to healthy tissue and should not be used for wound lavage, and surgical scrub agents are avoided because their detergent components damage tissue. A narrow tourniquet risks neurovascular complications, which is why a pressure wrap is preferred. Tight bandaging of a bleeding wound without veterinary direction also risks concealing continuing haemorrhage. Pressure, covering, documentation and escalation are the first aid actions the guidance supports.

depth.definitions: First aid is the immediate care given before definitive veterinary assessment and treatment. Lavage is washing of a wound with fluid to remove debris and reduce bacterial load. Debridement is the removal of nonviable tissue and foreign material. Contaminated describes a wound with bacterial load but no established infection, while dirty or infected describes a wound with established contamination or infection. An avulsion or degloving injury separates skin from underlying tissue. A pressure wrap provides circumferential pressure over a dressing, while a tourniquet encircles a limb and occludes flow. Moisture balance refers to keeping a wound bed appropriately moist while avoiding maceration of surrounding skin. Analgesia is pain relief, and it is a veterinary decision.
depth.mechanism: The organising principle of wound care in the manual is the combination of debridement, control of infection and inflammation, and moisture balance. Lavage supports that combination mechanically by diluting and washing out bacteria and debris, and it improves the examination of deeper tissue. The pressure used matters because flow energy drives particles out of tissue, but excessive pressure drives debris deeper and damages healing tissue, so the guidance specifies a range that is high enough to be useful and low enough to be safe, and it notes that tap water may be used to start on a large contaminated wound but is not ideal. Fluid choice matters because antiseptics act on bacterial cells and on the host cells that are trying to heal the wound, so a concentration that kills bacteria can also impair healing. Saline is the least toxic to healing tissue, dilute chlorhexidine diacetate retains activity while causing minimal tissue inflammation, povidone iodine has minimal residual activity and can be inactivated by purulent debris, and hydrogen peroxide is toxic to healthy tissue. Direct pressure controls bleeding by opposing the pressure in the injured vessel and allowing a clot to form, which is why pressure wraps preserve the neurovascular supply that a narrow tourniquet could compromise. Time matters because contamination increases the longer tissue is exposed, which is why the interval between injury and definitive debridement is minimised.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the stable dog with a fictional cat presented at 23:20 with a swollen, painful, discharging area over the base of the tail after a bite wound three days earlier. Here the surface appearance is the opposite of the terrier case: there is no fresh opening, yet there is an established infection, and the manual states that culture and susceptibility testing should be collected from infected wounds and that antimicrobial treatment should be instituted in dirty, infected or puncture wounds, with the choice of agent and the plan made by the veterinarian. The technician contribution changes from haemorrhage control to accurate history, warm compresses if directed, documentation, and support of the assessment. A second contrast is a fictional degloving injury over the carpus, where a full thickness skin loss exposes deeper tissue. The first aid actions are covering with a sterile dressing and immobilising the limb to protect the exposed tissue, followed by prompt veterinary assessment, because a wound of that class is not managed by dressing technique alone and requires surgical planning. Both examples show that the classification of the wound determines the boundary of what a technician does, and that in both classes the boundary stops before closure or drug selection.
depth.mistake: A widespread misconception is that vigorous cleaning with an antiseptic proves diligence. The manual specifically identifies surgical scrub agents and hydrogen peroxide as damaging to healing tissue, so a wound scrubbed enthusiastically can be worse off than one irrigated gently with saline at a controlled pressure. A second misconception is that a small hole is a small wound. Bite and puncture wounds are crush injuries with a small surface opening and a large area of compromised tissue underneath, and the manual treats dirty, infected and puncture wounds as warranting culture and antimicrobial treatment rather than observation. A third is that closing a wound early is always beneficial. Closing a contaminated wound can trap contamination and produce an abscess, which is why closure is a veterinary decision informed by contamination and timing. A fourth is the belief that stabilising the patient is a formality before wound care. The manual puts stability first precisely because dramatic wounds distract from shock, and an unnoticed perfusion problem kills faster than a dressed wound heals.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. For each of the following fictional presentations, state whether the wound is most likely a laceration, puncture, abrasion, avulsion or bite injury, whether it is clean or contaminated, and which first aid actions you would take within technician scope before passing the patient to the veterinarian. Presentation one: a 3 millimetre hole in a cat flank bite with surrounding swelling, sustained 40 minutes ago. Presentation two: a 6 centimetre linear cut on a dog hindlimb from a metal edge, bleeding briskly, dog alert with pink gums. Presentation three: extensive skin loss over the dorsal carpus after a road traffic accident, with the patient stable. Model response for presentation three: class as an avulsion with likely contamination, priority is stability confirmation and haemorrhage control, action is to cover with a sterile lint free dressing, immobilise as directed, keep the patient warm, document the mechanism and time, and escalate immediately for veterinary assessment. Self review rubric, four points. Did you classify using mechanism rather than appearance alone. Did you state whether stability was confirmed before wound care. Did you avoid any task outside technician scope such as probing, closing or selecting an antimicrobial. Did you record times and mechanisms rather than only describing the wound. Score one point per criterion.
depth.summary: Wounds are classified by mechanism, contamination and elapsed time, and the classification determines both the first aid that follows and the boundary of what a technician should do. Direct pressure, a pressure wrap rather than a narrow tourniquet, sterile covering, careful documentation and prompt escalation are the core first aid actions, while debridement, closure, culture interpretation and drug selection are veterinary work. The transferable principle is that assessment of the patient precedes assessment of the wound, because the wound that looks worst is not always the problem that threatens life.

visual.title: From mechanism to boundary: classifying a wound before acting
visual.description: A decision diagram that takes a wound through three questions, namely mechanism, contamination and elapsed time, and then maps each resulting class onto the first aid actions that are within technician scope and those that are not.
steps: Step one, check the patient before the wound: record heart rate, capillary refill time, mucous membrane colour and mentation, and escalate immediately if any of these suggest shock.
Step two, classify by mechanism: laceration, puncture, abrasion, avulsion or bite, noting that puncture and bite wounds hide deeper damage beneath a small opening.
Step three, classify by contamination and time: clean, contaminated, dirty or infected, with the interval since injury recorded in minutes.
Step four, act within scope: direct pressure, pressure wrap rather than narrow tourniquet for severe bleeding, sterile lint free covering, immobilisation if directed, warmth, and a timed report.

Step five, stop at the boundary: no probing or exploring, no removing embedded objects, no closure, no antiseptic scrubbing with surgical scrub or hydrogen peroxide, no antimicrobial selection, and hand over to the veterinarian.

questions.prompt: A fictional practice triages patients once at the door and does not reassess during the wait. Three patients have been waiting 40 minutes: a dog with a limp, a cat that has become progressively quieter with pale mucous membranes and a capillary refill time of three seconds, and a dog with one episode of diarrhoea that is eating. Which statement best describes the triage failure in this situation?
questions.answer: Triage is a repeating activity, so priority must be reassessed during the wait, because a patient can move from one category to another and the records of the cat now describe perfusion findings that require immediate veterinary evaluation
questions.distractor: There is no triage failure, because all three patients were correctly triaged at the door and the original categories remain valid until each patient is seen
questions.correction: Published triage guidance treats categorisation as provisional and expects reassessment as information changes. A single assessment at the door means the practice is prioritising a description that is 40 minutes old, and the cat with pale membranes and a prolonged capillary refill time is exactly the patient whose category has changed.

questions.prompt: A fictional cat arrives with an audible noise on inspiration, a respiratory rate of 56 per minute and a grey purple tongue edge. The practice has a plastic oxygen cage door that fits a cage across the room. Which choice best reflects the published guidance for this patient?
questions.answer: Start flow-by oxygen where the patient is and keep handling to the minimum while escalating immediately, because a cage limits access and delays reassessment in a patient whose stress level directly affects its oxygen demand
questions.distractor: Place the cat in the oxygen cage immediately, close the door, and reassess in twenty minutes, because containment reduces handling and time in oxygen can only help
questions.correction: The guidance describes oxygen cages as effective and low stress but notes that they restrict access and delay reassessment. For a patient in marked distress, access and continuous observation matter, so flow-by oxygen with minimal handling preserves both treatment and assessment.

questions.prompt: Two sets of observations on a fictional dog are 30 minutes apart. The first shows a heart rate of 180 with pale membranes and a capillary refill time of four seconds. The second shows a heart rate of 140 with unchanged pale membranes and the same capillary refill time. Which interpretation is most consistent with the physiology taught in this unit?
questions.answer: A falling heart rate in a patient whose perfusion findings have not improved is not reassurance and must be reported as a set with both times, because decompensation can include bradycardia, which cats in particular are noted to develop
questions.distractor: The heart rate has fallen towards the reference interval, which shows that the patient is improving, so the interval before the next check can safely be extended
questions.correction: Heart rate is one channel among several, and it cannot be interpreted without the perfusion findings beside it. A slower rate accompanying persistently poor perfusion reflects reduced cardiac output rather than recovery, and the published triage table notes that cats in particular develop bradycardia. Reporting the set with both timestamps is what allows the veterinarian to judge direction of travel.

questions.prompt: A fictional patient has been in cardiopulmonary arrest for about 90 seconds and compressions are in progress. The veterinarian asks for a 20 second pause so that a pulse can be palpated and a catheter placed. Which response best reflects the basic life support guidance?
questions.answer: Keep the interruption to the minimum possible, continuing compressions while the catheter is placed if that can be done safely, because compressions are specified as uninterrupted two minute cycles and perfusion pressure takes about a minute of continuous compressions to reach its maximum
questions.distractor: Pause for the full 20 seconds, because confirming a pulse and securing intravenous access are more valuable than a short delay in compressions
questions.correction: The guidance states that compressions should not be discontinued for procedures where that can be avoided, and it explains that about a minute of continuous compressions is required before myocardial perfusion pressure peaks. A 20 second pause therefore does more than cost 20 seconds of compressions; it resets a pressure curve that takes a minute to rebuild.

questions.prompt: A fictional client telephones about their stable dog, which has a 2 centimetre bite wound on the flank sustained 50 minutes ago, and asks whether they should clean it at home with hydrogen peroxide and wrap it tightly until tomorrow. Which advice and action best reflect the guidance in this unit?
questions.answer: Advise bringing the dog in now, explain that hydrogen peroxide is toxic to healing tissue and should not be used for wound lavage, cover the wound with a sterile lint free dressing if the client can, and record the mechanism and time of injury for the veterinarian
questions.distractor: Agree that hydrogen peroxide is a reasonable first step and that a firm bandage will control any contamination, and offer an appointment the following day if the wound looks worse
questions.correction: The wound manual states directly that hydrogen peroxide is toxic to healthy tissue and should not be used for lavage, and it treats bite and puncture wounds as contaminated injuries that warrant veterinary assessment and often culture. A tight bandage applied without veterinary direction conceals rather than manages the injury, and a 50 minute delay changes what options remain available.

lessons.title: Bandaging and splinting: principles, and the discipline of not bandaging
lessons.explanation: The word coaptation means bringing structures together, and in practice it refers to immobilising a limb with a sling, bandage, splint or cast. The veterinary literature states the goals of bandaging plainly: limiting haemorrhage, immobilising the area, preventing further trauma or contamination of the wound, preventing the wound from drying out, absorbing exudate, controlling infection, and aiding mechanical debridement. Those goals are achieved only if the bandage obeys a few principles. It should be adequately padded, applied evenly and snugly, built in three layers, and placed so that it does not traumatise new granulation tissue or epithelium. The primary or contact layer sits against the wound and allows fluid to pass to the secondary layer; it may be nonadherent, which minimises trauma and keeps the wound from drying out, or adherent, which incorporates debris into the dressing and removes it at the change, accepting that healthy tissue may be damaged too. The secondary layer absorbs fluid, pads the wound and supports or immobilises the limb, and is usually cast padding or roll cotton. The tertiary layer holds the first two in place, provides pressure and protects the inner layers from the environment. For first aid immobilisation of a limb, one rule dominates: the coaptation must immobilise the joint above and the joint below the injury, otherwise it adds weight to the distal limb without immobilising the fracture. Temporary immobilisation improves comfort, controls regional swelling, protects open wounds and can prevent a closed fracture from becoming an open one. Wounds must be treated according to open wound management principles before immobilisation, and a Robert Jones bandage is not suitable for injuries proximal to the elbow or stifle, where a spica splint is needed if coaptation is appropriate at all. Complications are the reason the discipline includes restraint about using bandages. Bandages that are too tight cause neurovascular compromise and tissue necrosis, and in some cases loss of a limb. Excess moisture in contact with healthy skin, including exudate, urine or faeces retained in the bandage, causes moisture associated skin damage. A study of 11 canine hindlimbs found that when a second clinician reapplied the bandage reusing the same fibreglass splint, 10 of the 11 bandages exceeded the study threshold of a 20 millimetre of mercury change in sub-bandage pressure at one or more locations, and that changes in pressure also occurred unpredictably when dogs moved from lateral recumbency to standing. Bandages therefore need scheduled inspection, and a wet, soiled, slipping or malodorous bandage needs veterinary reassessment rather than a wait until tomorrow. Choosing to bandage, choosing the materials and deciding when a bandage must come off are veterinary decisions; noticing, documenting and escalating bandage problems promptly are technician responsibilities.
lessons.example: A fictional greyhound has a lateral tarsal splint applied at 14:00 after a hock injury, and the technician is asked to check it at 18:00, 22:00 and 08:00 the next morning, which is three scheduled inspections in the first eighteen hours. The check is not a glance. It asks whether the bandage is still in place and intact, whether there is strike-through of fluid on the outer layer, whether the digits above and below are swollen, whether the toes are cool, whether the dog is comfortable, whether any odour is present, and whether the bandage has slipped. At 18:00 the toes are warm and dry, the bandage is intact and the dog is weight bearing. At 22:00 the toes are warm but the bandage has slipped distally by roughly a centimetre and there is a small damp patch on the outer layer. At 08:00 the toes are cool, the digits are swollen and the dog resists having the limb touched. Reasoning from the sources: a bandage that is too tight compromises neurovascular supply and can cause tissue necrosis, and damage can even lead to loss of the limb; pressure can also change after application, and the study of splint reapplication found a change in sub-bandage pressure in 10 of 11 bandages, which is 90.9 percent, when a different clinician reapplied the same splint. The technician does not cut the bandage off in a corridor without direction, and does not wait for the next scheduled check. The report is: 08:00, greyhound, tarsal splint, toes cool, digit swelling present, patient resenting handling, bandage slipped and damp, please assess now. The arithmetic of the schedule matters as much as the arithmetic of the study: three checks in eighteen hours means a problem could exist for ten hours between the 22:00 finding and the 08:00 finding, which is why the 22:00 slippage was itself reportable.
lessons.question: A fictional cat has a soft padded bandage over a distal antebrachial wound, applied four hours ago. The digits above the bandage are swollen and cool, and the cat is repeatedly licking at the bandage. Which response best reflects the principles of external coaptation?
lessons.answer: Report immediately for veterinary reassessment, describing the swelling, the temperature change, the licking and the time the bandage was applied, because these are features of a bandage that may be compromising the limb
lessons.distractor: Leave the bandage undisturbed until the next scheduled change tomorrow morning, and note the findings in the record, since removing or altering a bandage is not a technician task
lessons.correction: Cool digits, swelling and patient discomfort are the features the literature associates with excessive bandage pressure and neurovascular compromise, which the manual states can lead to tissue necrosis and, in some cases, loss of the limb. Waiting until a routine change converts an early, reversible problem into a late one. Not altering the bandage is correct; not reporting it is not.

depth.definitions: Coaptation is the immobilisation of a limb with an external sling, bandage, splint or cast. The primary or contact layer is the one touching the wound, the secondary layer absorbs and pads, and the tertiary layer secures and protects. An adherent dressing incorporates debris and removes it when changed, while a nonadherent dressing does not stick. A Robert Jones bandage is a soft, thickly padded bandage that uses no rigid splint material. A spica splint extends to the body to immobilise injuries above the elbow or stifle. Sub-bandage pressure is the pressure exerted by the bandage on the limb. Moisture associated skin damage is skin injury caused by prolonged contact with exudate, urine or faeces. Strike-through is fluid penetrating the outer bandage layer, which breaks the barrier.
depth.mechanism: A bandage is a mechanical system, so the outcome depends on force and geometry rather than on effort. Circumferential wraps generate pressure that is transmitted to the tissue beneath, and pressure is tolerated differently at different points, so uneven application creates focal high pressure areas while the rest of the limb is inadequately supported. Padding distributes force, which is why the manual requires sufficient padding, and rigidity controls movement, which is why splint material matters when immobilisation is the goal. Immobilising the joint above and below the injury works because a fracture moves when either adjacent joint moves; a splint that spans only one joint leaves the fracture mobile while adding mass and leverage. Limb swelling interacts with all of this, because tissue volume changes after injury and after bandaging, and the study of splint reapplication showed pressure changes were both common on reapplication and unpredictable with posture. That combination, variable pressure plus a closed system nobody can see into, is why scheduled inspection rather than faith is the safety mechanism. Complications therefore have a common pathway: either pressure is too high and perfusion falls, or moisture is trapped and skin barrier function fails.
depth.secondExample: Contrast the tarsal splint with a fictional dog that has had a large contaminated laceration over the elbow debrided under anaesthesia and dressed with a wet-to-dry contact layer. Bandaging here is being used for a different purpose, which is debridement and exudate management rather than immobilisation, and the relevant hazard is different: the dressing is intentionally adherent and painful to remove, and the manual notes that it debrides appreciably but also that healthy tissue may be damaged. The technician task is therefore timing and comfort, keeping the scheduled change on time and supporting analgesia as directed, rather than checking for slipping. A second contrast is a fictional cat with a closed, clean surgical incision that a client asks to have bandaged for reassurance. There is no haemorrhage, no contamination, no immobilisation requirement and no exudate to manage, so the bandage would add pressure risk and hide the wound from inspection while serving none of the stated goals. Deciding not to bandage is a clinical decision with a real justification, and the technician who understands the goals of bandaging can describe why.
depth.mistake: A widespread misconception is that a snug bandage should be tight to control swelling. The manual states the opposite result: bandages that are too tight cause neurovascular compromise and tissue necrosis, and swelling control comes from even, adequately padded pressure rather than from constriction. A second misconception is that a comfortable patient proves a safe bandage, because sensation may be reduced and because animals tolerate a great deal before showing distress. Inspection of the digits, the outer layer and the odour is what detects problems, not the absence of complaint. A third misconception is that a bandage left unchanged is a bandage left undisturbed, when in fact the literature on reapplication shows pressure behaviour changing with person, time and posture. A fourth is that any bandage is better than none for a limb injury, which ignores that a poorly placed coaptation can leave the fracture mobile, add weight and convert a closed fracture into an open one.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Write a bandage check protocol for a fictional small animal practice on one page, containing the items to be checked, the minimum frequency, the findings that must be escalated immediately, and the wording of the escalation. Then complete a self audit on three fictional records provided in the course materials. Model content for the escalation list: the digits are cool or swollen, the bandage has slipped, the outer layer is damp from strike-through, there is an odour, the patient is licking or chewing at the bandage, or the patient is not using the limb as before. Model escalation wording: 08:00, greyhound, left tarsal splint applied 14:00 yesterday, toes cool, digits swollen, bandage slipped distally, patient resenting handling, please assess now. Self review rubric, five points. Did you include both an inspection list and a frequency. Did you distinguish observations from conclusions. Did you state a time in the escalation. Did you include the possibility that the right action is veterinary reassessment rather than re-bandaging. Did you specify who receives the report rather than an unspecified team. Score one point per criterion.
depth.summary: Bandaging is a mechanical intervention with defined goals, a three layer structure and a specific immobilisation rule about spanning the joints above and below an injury. Its hazards are pressure and moisture, its behaviour changes with time, posture and the person applying it, and its safety depends on scheduled inspection and prompt escalation. The most mature skill in this topic is recognising when a bandage serves none of its goals and therefore should not be applied, and that judgement is made by the veterinarian.
